title: Twenty-Four Cousins — species dataset
notes: Numeric fields are literature values; each species lists the sources used.
The 'traits' block is carried over from the Kaggle teaching dataset (qualitative, categorical) and has not been independently verified.
The species list follows the Kaggle dataset (24 names). Several are lumped by many researchers: see each 'status'.
'found' is the year the first fossils were recovered; 'named' is the year the species name was published.

SI.label: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, species pages

AM.label: Australian Museum, Human Evolution species pages

LEBATARD2008.label: Lebatard et al. 2008, PNAS 105:3226, cosmogenic dating of Sahelanthropus and Australopithecus bahrelghazali

FERRING2011.label: Ferring et al. 2011, PNAS 108:10432, earliest occupations at Dmanisi 1.85–1.78 Ma

LORD2013.label: Lordkipanidze et al. 2013, Science 342:326, Dmanisi Skull 5 (D4500), 546 cc

LORD2007.label: Lordkipanidze et al. 2007, Nature 449:305, Dmanisi postcrania, stature 145–166 cm

GRUN2020.label: Grün et al. 2020, Nature 580:372, Broken Hill (Kabwe 1) dated 299 ± 25 ka

KAGGLE.label: Kaggle 'Biological Data of Human Ancestors' (santiago123678), 720-row teaching dataset; qualitative trait columns only

species.name: Sahelanthropus tchadensis

time.note: Smithsonian: 'sometime between 7 and 6 million years ago'; cosmogenic dating of the TM 266 level gives 7.04–6.83 Ma (Lebatard et al. 2008).

cranial_cc.note: Estimated from the distorted Toumaï cranium; Australian Museum gives 320–380 cc.

height_cm.note: No limb bones securely assigned; body size probably chimpanzee-like (Smithsonian).

species.fact: The oldest known hominin — its skull, nicknamed Toumaï, hints at upright posture nearly 7 million years ago.
species.status: Widely accepted; bipedality debated.

species.name: Orrorin tugenensis

time.note: Smithsonian: 'sometime between 6.2 and 5.8 million years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: No cranial remains.

height_cm.note: Chimpanzee-sized; body mass estimated at 30–50 kg from femur and humerus (Smithsonian).

species.fact: Femur fragments suggest Orrorin walked upright while still climbing trees — a dual-purpose ape.
species.status: Widely accepted.

species.name: Ardipithecus ramidus

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 4.4 million years ago'; Aramis horizon 4.4 Ma, Gona 4.5–4.3 Ma.

cranial_cc.note: Ardi (ARA-VP-6/500) cranium estimated at 300–350 cc (Australian Museum).

species.fact: Ardi's foot had a grasping toe yet she walked on two legs — bipedalism evolved in forests, not savannas.
species.status: Widely accepted.

species.name: Australopithecus anamensis
species.type_site: Kanapoi and Allia Bay, Lake Turkana

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 4.2 to 3.8 million years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: From the MRD cranium (Woranso-Mille, 2016): about 365–370 cc (Australian Museum).

height_cm.note: Possibly the size of a female chimpanzee (Smithsonian).

species.fact: The earliest known australopith, with a tibia clearly built for upright walking.
species.status: Widely accepted.

species.name: Australopithecus bahrelghazali

time.note: Cosmogenic 10Be/9Be date of the KT 12 level: 3.58 ± 0.27 Ma (Lebatard et al. 2008); shown as the 2σ range.

cranial_cc.note: Known only from a mandible and a premolar; no cranium.

species.fact: Found 2,500 km west of the Rift Valley — the only australopith from central Africa.
species.status: Validity disputed; many researchers assign the material to Au. afarensis.

species.name: Australopithecus afarensis

time.note: Smithsonian: 'between about 3.85 and 2.95 million years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: Average about 430 cc (Australian Museum); Smithsonian: 'usually less than 500 cc'.

species.fact: Lucy's species. The Laetoli footprints prove they walked the savanna upright 3.6 million years ago.
species.status: Widely accepted.

species.name: Australopithecus africanus

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: Average about 480 cc (Australian Museum); adult specimens span roughly 400–560 cc.

species.fact: The Taung Child was the first australopith ever found, and the fossil that revealed Africa as humanity's cradle.
species.status: Widely accepted.

species.name: Paranthropus aethiopicus

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 2.7 to 2.3 million years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: KNM-WT 17000: 410 cc (Smithsonian fossil page). Only one measurable cranium.

species.fact: The 'Black Skull' had the largest sagittal crest of any hominin — anchoring jaws that could crush nuts.
species.status: Widely accepted; named from the 1967 Omo mandible, the Black Skull was found in 1985.

species.name: Australopithecus garhi

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 2.5 million years ago'; drawn as a short bar because only one horizon is known.

cranial_cc.note: About 450 cc (Australian Museum). One partial cranium.

species.fact: Found alongside butchered antelope bones — possibly the first known toolmaker.
species.status: Accepted; association with butchered bones is debated.

species.name: Homo habilis

time.note: Smithsonian: '2.4 million to 1.4 million years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: Average about 610 cc; KNM-ER 1813 is 510 cc (Australian Museum).

species.fact: 'Handy man' — the first hominin associated with stone tools, the Oldowan industry.
species.status: Widely accepted; membership in Homo debated.

species.name: Paranthropus boisei

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 2.3 to 1.2 million years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: KNM-ER 406 about 510 cc; OH 5 about 530 cc; species values cluster around 500–550 cc.

species.fact: Nicknamed 'Nutcracker Man' for molars four times the size of ours — built to grind tough plants.
species.status: Widely accepted.

species.name: Australopithecus sediba

time.note: Smithsonian: 'between 1.977 and 1.98 million years ago'; a single, tightly dated deposit.

cranial_cc.note: MH1 estimated at about 420 cc (Australian Museum).

species.fact: A mosaic of ape and human traits — its hand could precision-grip, but its arms were still built for climbing.
species.status: Accepted; some treat it as late Au. africanus.

species.name: Homo rudolfensis

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 1.9 million to 1.8 million years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: KNM-ER 1470: about 775 cc (Smithsonian); average about 750 cc (Australian Museum).

height_cm.note: Unknown; no securely associated limb bones (Smithsonian).

species.fact: A larger-brained contemporary of H. habilis — early Homo was a bushy tree, not a single line.
species.status: Accepted by many; some lump it with H. habilis.

species.name: Homo ergaster

time.note: Core group 1.9–1.5 Ma (Australian Museum); African material spans about 1.9–1.4 Ma.

cranial_cc.note: Average about 860 cc (Australian Museum); KNM-ER 42700 about 690 cc; Turkana Boy about 880 cc, projected 910 cc as an adult.

height_cm.note: Females about 160 cm, males about 180 cm (Australian Museum); Turkana Boy projected 1.8 m or more.

species.fact: Modern body proportions and Acheulean handaxes — the first hominin who looked, from the neck down, like us.
species.status: Often treated as early African Homo erectus (Smithsonian).

species.name: Homo erectus

time.note: Smithsonian: 'between about 1.89 million and 110,000 years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: Average about 1,050 cc (Australian Museum); adult crania span roughly 750–1,250 cc.

species.fact: The longest-lived human species — nearly 2 million years across Africa and Asia, and the first to use fire.
species.status: Widely accepted; the longest-lived human species.

species.name: Homo georgicus

time.note: Site occupation 1.85–1.78 Ma; hominin fossils about 1.77 Ma (Ferring et al. 2011).

cranial_cc.note: Five crania: D4500 546 cc (Lordkipanidze et al. 2013), D2700 about 600, D2282 about 650, D2280 about 780 cc.

height_cm.note: Stature 145–166 cm from Dmanisi postcrania (Lordkipanidze et al. 2007).

species.fact: Found at Dmanisi — the earliest hominin remains outside Africa, a small-brained pioneer.
species.status: Most researchers now classify the Dmanisi fossils as Homo erectus (H. e. georgicus).

species.name: Paranthropus robustus

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 1.8 to 1.2 million years ago'; Drimolen material pushes the origin to about 2.0 Ma.

cranial_cc.note: Species average about 530 cc; SK 1585 endocast 476 cc.

height_cm.note: Females about 100 cm, males about 120 cm (Smithsonian).

species.fact: A robust australopith that lived alongside early Homo — and lost the evolutionary race.
species.status: Widely accepted.

species.name: Homo antecessor

time.note: About 1.2–0.8 Ma (Australian Museum); the TD6 fossils are about 0.85–0.78 Ma.

cranial_cc.note: Approximately 1,000 cc, estimated from the juvenile type specimen (Australian Museum).

species.fact: Europe's earliest known human — and the first to leave evidence of cannibalism.
species.status: Accepted; its place relative to H. heidelbergensis and H. sapiens is debated.

species.name: Homo heidelbergensis

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 700,000 to 200,000 years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: Average about 1,250 cc (Australian Museum); Steinheim 1,110–1,200 cc, Kabwe about 1,300 cc.

species.fact: Big-brained big-game hunters — the likely ancestor of both Neanderthals and us.
species.status: Widely used; a 'wastebasket' taxon for Middle Pleistocene humans.

species.name: Homo rhodesiensis

time.note: Kabwe 1 is 299 ± 25 ka (Grün et al. 2020; Smithsonian gives 324,000–274,000); Bodo, the other key African cranium, is about 600 ka.

cranial_cc.note: Kabwe 1 about 1,300 cc (Smithsonian fossil page; 1,280 cc in the Australian Museum entry).

height_cm.note: Associated tibia suggests a tall individual, but no reliable species figure.

species.fact: Sometimes considered an African Heidelbergensis — a possible ancestor of modern humans.
species.status: Usually folded into H. heidelbergensis; some now use H. bodoensis for the African material.

species.name: Homo neanderthalensis

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 400,000 – 40,000 years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: Average about 1,450–1,500 cc (Australian Museum); Amud 1 is 1,740 cc.

species.fact: Cold-adapted Europeans who buried their dead, made art, and live on in 1–4% of non-African DNA.
species.status: Widely accepted; interbred with H. sapiens.

species.name: Homo naledi

time.note: Smithsonian: '335,000–236,000 years ago'.

cranial_cc.note: Females about 465 cc, males about 560 cc, LES1 about 610 cc (Australian Museum).

height_cm.note: Approximately 1.44 m (Smithsonian); adult males about 150 cm (Australian Museum).

species.fact: Small-brained yet possibly buried its dead in deep cave chambers — a stunning recent discovery.
species.status: Widely accepted; claims of deliberate burial are contested.

species.name: Homo sapiens
species.type_site: Oldest fossils: Jebel Irhoud, Morocco (about 300 ka)

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 300,000 years ago to present'.

cranial_cc.note: Average approximately 1,300 cc (Smithsonian); normal adult range roughly 1,100–1,500 cc.

height_cm.note: Present-day global adult averages, roughly 159 cm (women) and 171 cm (men).

species.fact: Us. The only surviving human lineage out of more than two dozen — and now the most populous large mammal on Earth.
species.status: The one surviving species. 'Found' refers to the Jebel Irhoud discovery; the species was named by Linnaeus in 1758.

species.name: Homo floresiensis

time.note: Smithsonian: 'about 100,000 – 50,000 years ago' (fossils about 100,000–60,000).

cranial_cc.note: LB1 about 426 cc; Australian Museum gives 380–420 cc.

height_cm.note: 106 cm, estimated from the LB1 female skeleton (Smithsonian).

species.fact: The 'Hobbit' — a meter-tall human that survived on Flores until perhaps 50,000 years ago.
species.status: Widely accepted as a distinct dwarfed species.
